Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Julian had been on the scaffolding when the steel coupling snapped. He watched the concrete slab drop, saw the man’s leg twist at a wrong angle, and felt the sudden, heavy pressure on his own shoulders as he rushed to help stabilize the fallen timber. The event’s specific sensory imprint—the weight on his shoulders, the sharp metallic tang of blood mixing with sawdust, the wide visual of the torn shirt and weeping wound—remains potent because it mirrors the exact qualities of that afternoon, leaving his present surroundings perpetually charged. Over the following weeks, Julian’s world narrowed. He had come to believe that the ground beneath him could no longer hold steady, and what frightened him most was the feeling that his life had been permanently destroyed. He was certain that something vital had cracked inside him, a change that would not heal. He found himself avoiding thinking about the incident altogether, steering conversations away from job sites, away from the very wood and metal that once felt familiar. In the present, the triggers arrive without warning. A client’s damp hand brushing his forearm while handing over a contract sends a sudden wave through him. He does not just remember; the memory drops over him completely, flooding his senses as if the slab is falling again, the specific taste of copper and burnt sugar on his tongue, the weight pressing down, the sight of the wound stark and raw. His nonverbal memory surfaces not as a story he tells, but as a tightness in his chest that refuses a narrative. When the flood feels too heavy, he deliberately leaves his body, blanking out until the noise of the workshop fades to a dull hum. To quiet the restlessness that settles in his chest, he eats excessively, finishing the entire tray of sandwiches his wife leaves on the counter, not from hunger but to manage the distress. His wife, Elena, notices how he retreats into himself, how he flinches when she reaches for his hand, how he keeps his eyes on his tools to avoid the thought of what happened. His occupation, once his anchor, has become a landscape of potential threat. At his carpentry bench, he measures twice but cuts slowly, convinced that his hands no longer respond with the precision they once did. He cannot rely on himself to judge the weight of a plank or the tension of a cable. The visual trigger of a fresh wound on a helper’s forearm makes his stomach turn, pulling him back into that afternoon on the scaffolding. He eats through the distress, the excess food settling heavily in his stomach, while his deliberate blanking out leaves him disconnected from the day. He and Elena have grown apart in the quiet ways; she speaks to him, but he hears her voice as if from underwater, certain that he is permanently changed, no longer the man who held the space steady. His life feels dismantled, piece by piece, the way a house frame comes apart when the foundation shifts. Now, at thirty, Julian sits in the therapist’s office, his calloused hands resting on his knees, still carrying the invisible weight of the fall. He has come to believe that the memory will swallow him whole if he lets it, and he avoids the thought to keep it at bay. His work has slowed; the careful pacing takes extra hours, and the excess eating adds a heaviness to his step. Elena has asked him to come, and he has agreed, hoping for something he cannot quite name. He is most afraid of the sudden touch, the unexpected taste, the sight of a wound that might send him right back. He hopes, perhaps, to find a way to stand on solid ground again without having to leave himself behind. His North American upbringing, steeped in the practical rhythms of family and work, runs parallel to these symptoms, neither driving them nor being driven by them.
